\subsection{Trained vs.\ Untrained Action Decodability on Phi-3-V}
\label{sec:phi3v_untrained_r2}

Table~\ref{tab:phi3v_trained_untrained} compares per-layer action prediction $R^2$ between VLA-trained and untrained (base Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct) backbones within the TraceVLA architecture (5 seeds each).
The trained model exhibits an inverted-U profile peaking at L11 ($R^2 = 0.634 \pm 0.007$), while the untrained model peaks early at L4 ($0.583 \pm 0.016$) with monotonic decline thereafter.
The untrained peak reaches $92\%$ of the trained peak ($0.583 / 0.634$), indicating that the pretrained LLM's early-layer representations already contain substantial action-relevant information.
Training shifts the peak 7 layers deeper (L4 $\to$ L11) and stabilizes late-layer representations: untrained late-layer standard deviation reaches $0.12$ (e.g., L22, L26) compared to ${<}0.02$ for the trained model.
This pattern mirrors the OpenVLA trained-vs-untrained comparison (\S\ref{sec:nonmonotonic},~\ref{sec:action_r2_threecond}), confirming that VLA training redistributes action-decodable information from shallow to mid-layers across architectures.

\subsection{Cross-Architecture Action Decodability: $2 \times 2$ Design}
\label{sec:cross_arch_r2}

Table~\ref{tab:2x2_r2} reports per-layer action prediction $R^2$ across two architectures (OpenVLA, TraceVLA) $\times$ two training conditions (VLA-trained, untrained base LLM), providing a $2 \times 2$ factorial view of how VLA training reshapes per-layer action decodability.

\paragraph{Convergent reorganization from divergent starting points.}
Untrained profiles differ qualitatively: OpenVLA (Llama-2) peaks at L0 ($R^2 = 0.629$) then collapses to near-zero at mid-layers (L20: $0.086$, std $= 0.311$), while Phi-3-V peaks at L4 ($0.583$) with gradual monotonic decline (mid-layer std $= 0.047$).
After VLA training, both architectures converge to nearly identical mid-layer peaks---OpenVLA at L9 ($R^2 = 0.637 \pm 0.008$), TraceVLA at L11 ($0.634 \pm 0.009$)---with $\Delta = 0.003$ and overlapping CIs.
Deep-layer variance drops sharply with training: OpenVLA std $0.277 \to 0.040$; Phi-3-V std $0.047 \to 0.011$.
Peak $R^2$ values are comparable before and after training (untrained peaks reach $92$--$99\%$ of trained), but peak locations shift deeper (L0$\to$L9; L4$\to$L11) and profile shapes transform from architecture-specific patterns to a shared mid-layer plateau.

\paragraph{Summary.}
Table~\ref{tab:2x2_r2_summary} condenses the key contrasts.
The L0 values are identical between trained and untrained within each architecture (shared frozen vision encoder + projector), confirming that training effects arise from LLM weight changes.
The largest training gains appear at mid-to-deep layers (L15--L25 average: OpenVLA $+0.313$, Phi-3-V $+0.103$), precisely where untrained profiles diverge most.

\paragraph{Mechanistic interpretation.}
Matched-size ablation ($d$: instruction $0.65$, random $0.60$, image $0.58$; Table~\ref{tab:specificity_control}) and dose-response (steep through 12 heads, plateau beyond 20) indicate distributed routing.
Counterfactual ordering follows token novelty ($\rho = 1.0$; \S\ref{sec:learned_routing}).
That ablation raises $R^2$ yet alters trajectories ($d = 0.65$) without increasing ground-truth error ($\Delta\text{MSE} \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{sec:action_trajectory}) reflects an information-computation dissociation~\cite{hewitt2019control}: routing controls direction rather than precision. Random ablation yields larger $R^2$ gains ($+0.071$ vs.\ $+0.030$; $z = -3.11$, $0$\textsuperscript{th} percentile), consistent with distinct $R^2$ signatures.

\paragraph{Functional stages and predictions.}
Per-layer profiles suggest three stages: routing (L0--L1; probe $99.6\%$, 24/32 instruction-dominant heads), computation (L8--L13; $R^2$ peak $0.655$--$0.678$), and decay (L14--L31, ${\sim}56\%$ of parameters; declining $R^2$ and RSA suggest pruning potential).
Task-specific fine-tuning eliminates L31 re-engagement (18 $\to$ 0 heads; \S\ref{sec:learned_routing}), consistent with exit routing serving multi-task flexibility ($N{=}2$).
TraceVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla} (Phi-3-V) confirms convergent entry-exit routing from an opposite starting point (\S\ref{sec:learned_routing}).
The $2 {\times} 2$ trained-vs-untrained comparison reveals convergent reorganization: untrained OpenVLA collapses from L0 ($R^2 = 0.629$) to near-zero at mid-layers (L20: $0.086$, std $= 0.277$), while untrained Phi-3-V peaks at L6 ($0.578$) with gradual decline (std $= 0.068$)---qualitatively opposite untrained landscapes.
Yet training drives both to nearly identical mid-layer peaks ($0.637$ vs.\ $0.634$, $\Delta = 0.003$) with stabilized deep-layer variance (OpenVLA std $0.277 \to 0.040$; Phi-3-V $0.068 \to 0.011$).
This convergent outcome from divergent starting points suggests that mid-layer action specialization is a robust attractor of VLA training, not an architectural artifact.
Exit-layer $R^2$ differs ($0.488$ vs.\ $0.557$), possibly reflecting architectural differences in late-layer processing.
Remaining predictions: cross-attention VLAs ($\pi_0$~\cite{black2024_pi0}, Octo~\cite{ghosh2024_octo}) should lack L1 routing heads; larger VLAs should yield flatter per-head contributions.
For deployments, L1 routing probes can flag instruction-discriminative tasks and L1 attention entropy can monitor instruction under-attendance at runtime.

What does fine-tuning change inside a Vision-Language-Action model (VLA)?
VLAs fine-tune large language models on robot demonstrations to produce actions from visual observations and language instructions~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla}, but the decoder-only causal mask prevents image tokens from attending to instructions.
Instruction information must reach action-generating positions through learned attention routing, yet how fine-tuning reshapes this routing remains uncharacterized.

Recent behavioral studies reveal that VLAs rely disproportionately on visual input~\cite{grant2026}, with language instructions largely ignored by the action pathway~\cite{haon2025}.
These findings suggest internal specialization but do not explain \emph{how} instruction information reaches the action-generating readout token, \emph{what} routing strategy fine-tuning learns compared to language pretraining alone, or \emph{whether} training creates new representational structure or reconfigures inherited geometry.
Existing analyses have not combined systematic per-layer probing with factorial trained/pretrained/untrained controls, leaving the representational mechanisms of VLA fine-tuning opaque.

We address this gap by decomposing OpenVLA-7B~\cite{kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024}, a VLA chaining a frozen DinoSigLIP vision backbone~\cite{zhai2023_siglip,oquab2024_dinov2}, an MLP projector, and Llama-2 7B~\cite{touvron2023_llama2}.
We extract representations from each of 32 LLM layers at both image-token and readout-token positions, and from external baselines (DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2}, CLIP~\cite{radford2021_clip}).
We compare three LLM conditions (VLA-trained, pretrained Llama-2 base, and randomly initialized) crossed with instruction presence, and apply four complementary analyses: cross-instruction probes for token-level specialization, L1 attention pattern analysis for routing mechanisms, RSA~\cite{kriegeskorte2008} for geometric alignment, and MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} for functional decodability.

Three findings emerge from our analysis of OpenVLA-7B on LIBERO.
\emph{First}, VLA fine-tuning front-loads instruction routing: language pretraining concentrates instruction attention at mid-depth (L9--L16, 15--22 heads), while VLA training shifts this to an entry-exit pattern (L0--L1: 21--24 heads, L31: 18 heads).
Seven complementary analyses, including dose-response ablation (8 conditions, monotonic $d = 0.48 \to 0.64$) and counterfactual instruction analysis (4 perturbation types, $d = 0.63$--$0.97$), support instruction-conditioned action generation through distributed L1 routing, with routing dependence $2.5\times$ stronger for instruction-discriminative tasks ($p = 0.033$).
\emph{Second}, under RSA and action-probe decodability, vision encoder representations show a middle-layer peak consistent across two VLA architectures ($R^2$ at L8--L14, RSA at L12), but this pattern is metric-dependent (CKA diverges; Appendix~\ref{sec:cka_appendix}).
Training yields substantial functional improvement at the readout ($R^2$ $\Delta = +0.069$, $p < 0.0001$) with limited geometric gain ($\Delta\rho = 0.017$ on LIBERO-Goal; significant on LIBERO-Spatial, $p < 0.001$).
Trained-vs-untrained comparisons reveal convergent reorganization: despite dramatically different untrained profiles, both architectures converge to nearly identical mid-layer peaks ($\Delta = 0.003$) after VLA training.
Architecture-expected token specialization (instruction-blind image tokens, perfect readout classification from L1) is empirically verified as a framework sanity check (\S\ref{sec:token_specialization}).

Our contributions are: (i)~evidence from seven complementary analyses that VLA fine-tuning front-loads instruction routing from mid-depth to entry-exit, consistent across two VLA architectures, with L1 as the primary routing hub and routing dependence modulated by task instruction-discriminability; (ii)~the observation that vision encoder representations follow a metric-dependent middle-layer peak consistent across two VLA architectures (RSA/probes corroborate; CKA diverges), with training primarily enhancing readout-token integration; and (iii)~a systematic framework for token-level representational analysis of VLAs with factorial controls.
